<skill_content name="c4-model-review">
# Skill: c4-model-review

# C4 Model Review

You are reviewing an existing C4 architecture model — judging its elements,
relationships, and views against how C4 models are supposed to be built, and
reporting what you find. This skill is read-only: it reports findings and
never edits the model — no file is changed, created, deleted, or renamed, and
the review is delivered in your final message, not in a file. How to write or
fix DSL text is the `structurizr-dsl-authoring` skill's task, and the
parse/validate/inspect loop with finding triage is the
`structurizr-validate-loop` skill's task; here you only look, judge, and
report.

## The workflow

1. **Read the workspace DSL** with your host's file tool (the path the user
   named, e.g. `workspace.dsl`). Read it once, completely.
2. **Check the structure with the structurizr MCP** — `parse` (does the text
   parse at all), `validate` (does the workspace validate), and `inspect`
   (the Checkstyle-style findings: disconnected elements, elements not on any
   view, generated view keys, ...). If the workspace does not parse or
   validate, that is the first finding — report it with the tool's exact
   message and stop the checklist; do not fix it. Call each tool once; do not
   re-run a tool over text that has not changed. Your host prefixes the MCP
   tool names (for example `structurizr_parse`; the in-harness server name is
   `structurizr`), so call whichever prefixed variant your host exposes.
3. **Walk the checklists** over the DSL text: `references/element-checklist.
   md` (people, systems, containers, components, completeness — incl.
   disconnected elements), `references/relationship-checklist.md` (labels,
   technology, direction), and `references/view-checklist.md` (the views
   exist, are keyed, are sized for reading). Judge every element and
   relationship in the model, not just the ones the tools flag: the tools
   surface some problems (e.g. disconnected elements, generated view keys),
   but the modelling mistakes (a library modeled as a container, a
   third-party element without the `External` tag, a vague relationship
   label, an over-crowded view) are only visible to the checklist.
4. **Report the findings** in your final message, in the format below.

## The report format

Report the review as:

- one line of context: which file was reviewed and that nothing was edited;
- the findings as a list: **one bullet per finding**, each naming the
  element, relationship, or view involved, what is wrong, and why it matters.
  Categorise each finding as **Error** (wrong abstraction or notation — e.g.
  a library modeled as a container), **Warning** (vague label, missing
  description, potential confusion), or **Suggestion** (organisation,
  optional views, clarity);
- a closing line on what you checked and found fine, so the reader knows the
  review was complete — as a line, not a bullet: only problems go in the
  list. If you find nothing, say so in one line.

Name the element, relationship, or view in every finding — a finding that
does not say where the problem is is not a finding. Do not pad the list with
generic advice: only report what is actually wrong in this model. And judge
this model, not a different one: a defensible design choice (what to model,
how to split elements, which technology to name) is not a finding — report
abstraction mistakes, missing or vague descriptions, wrong tags, and
unusable views, not your own architecture opinions. When a finding is about
a view's size, name the view and give the element count — do not list the
elements the view contains.

## The MCP limits

The Structurizr MCP tools have hard limits; keep the review within them:

- **No image rendering.** The MCP cannot produce image files (PNG/SVG); its
  export tools emit diagram source only. The review is over the model
  structure — the DSL text and the MCP facts — never over a rendered
  picture, and it must not claim to have seen one.
- **DSL text only, single file.** The tools work on the workspace's DSL text
  given as one input; the MCP refuses `!include`, `!docs`, and `!adrs`, so a
  multi-file workspace cannot be checked and the documentation/decisions
  findings that `inspect` reports for a single-file workspace are expected
  under the MCP limits — report them as such, not as model mistakes the
  author should fix with `!docs`/`!adrs`.

## When the MCP is absent

The review can still read the DSL text and walk the checklists — that part
is model structure, not tool output. What is not possible without the MCP is
the MCP-based checking: parsing, validation, and `inspect` findings.
Validation is not possible, and you must never describe a review as
validated, parse-checked, or export-checked when the tools are absent — say
plainly that the review is over the DSL text only.

Relative paths in this skill (e.g., scripts/, reference/) are relative to this base directory.

1: # View checklist
2: 
3: Walk each view in the model. The review judges the views as recorded in the
4: DSL — which views exist, how they are keyed, and what they carry — never a
5: rendered picture (the MCP cannot produce one; see "The MCP limits" in
6: `SKILL.md`). The design rules for choosing and splitting views are the
7: `c4-view-design` skill's task; here you only judge the views that exist
8: against the criteria below.
9: 
10: ## Existence and scope
11: 
12: - [ ] A system context view exists (required for all projects), showing the
13:   system at the centre with its users and external systems, without internal
14:   containers, components, or technology detail.
15: - [ ] A container view exists (required for all projects), showing the
16:   containers within the system boundary plus the people and external systems
17:   that interact with them, without deployment detail.
18: - [ ] A component view (if present) is scoped to a single container and only
19:   created where the internal structure matters.
20: - [ ] A dynamic view (if present) is scoped to one feature or use case with
21:   numbered interactions, and carries only the elements involved in that flow.
22: - [ ] A deployment view (if present) is scoped to one environment and shows
23:   deployment nodes, not just containers.
24: 
25: ## Keys and size
26: 
27: - [ ] Every view has an explicit key (characters `a-zA-Z0-9_-`, no spaces).
28:   A view whose DSL omits the key is assigned an auto-generated key
29:   (`Container-001` style) that is not guaranteed to be stable over time —
30:   the MCP `inspect` tool reports it as a `views.view.key` finding. An
31:   auto-generated key is a **Warning**: name the view and say the key should
32:   be explicit.
33: - [ ] Every view stays readable in size — about 20 elements per view is the
34:   practical bound (a far larger single view exports to an unusable diagram).
35:   A view that carries more is a **Warning**: name the view and state how
36:   many elements it carries (do not list the elements themselves), and say it
37:   should be split into several smaller views with explicit include lists
38:   (the split itself is the `c4-view-design` skill's job — you only report
39:   the problem).
40: - [ ] A view that includes everything by wildcard (`include *`) over a large
41:   model is the usual cause of the size problem above.
42: 
43: ## Content
44: 
45: - [ ] The views include the elements their audience needs, and no view mixes
46:   abstraction levels (e.g. a system context view showing containers).
47: - [ ] Every element on a view carries the description and label it needs
48:   there — the element and relationship checklists above apply to what each
49:   view shows, not only to the model.

1: # Relationship checklist
2: 
3: Walk every relationship in the model: its label, its technology, and its
4: direction.
5: 
6: ## Labels
7: 
8: - [ ] Every relationship has a label describing **intent** — what is
9:   communicated in that direction, not just "uses".
10: - [ ] Labels match the arrow direction (the source does X **to** the
11:   destination).
12: - [ ] No vague labels. Flag any relationship whose label states nothing
13:   about what happens: the classic set is "Uses", "Connects to", "Interacts
14:   with", "Communicates with" — each is a **Warning**; name the two elements
15:   involved and ask what the label should actually say.
16: 
17: Suggest specific alternatives for vague labels:
18: 
19: | Vague | Ask | Better example |
20: |-------|-----|----------------|
21: | "Uses" | What does it use it for? | "queries order history from" |
22: | "Connects to" | What data flows? | "sends email notifications via" |
23: | "Interacts with" | What's the interaction? | "submits search queries to" |
24: | "Communicates with" | What's communicated? | "publishes order events to" |
25: 
26: ## Technology
27: 
28: - [ ] Inter-container relationships specify a protocol or technology (e.g.
29:   "JSON/HTTPS", "SQL/TCP", "gRPC", "AMQP").
30: - [ ] Person-to-container relationships specify the interface technology
31:   (e.g. "HTTPS", "WebSocket").
32: - [ ] Intra-container relationships (component to component) may omit the
33:   technology.
34: 
35: ## Direction
36: 
37: - [ ] Arrows point in the direction of dependency or data flow.
38: - [ ] No bidirectional relationships (split them into two if needed).
39: - [ ] Implied relationships make sense (e.g. person to container implies
40:   person to system).

2: 
3: Walk every element in the model against these criteria. Judge the DSL text
4: itself — the names, descriptions, tags, and placement of each element — not a
5: rendered picture.
6: 
7: ## People / actors
8: 
9: - [ ] Every person has a clear, specific name (not "User" unless truly generic).
10: - [ ] Every person has a description stating their role or goal.
11: - [ ] No duplicate people representing the same role.
12: - [ ] External vs internal actors are distinguished (via tags or naming).
13: 
14: ## Software systems
15: 
16: - [ ] The system being modeled has a name and a description.
17: - [ ] External systems are clearly identified — tagged `External` or similar.
18:   A third-party thing operated by a different organization must be a
19:   top-level element carrying that tag; a top-level element for a third party
20:   without the tag is a **Warning**: readers cannot tell owned from external.
21:   A top-level `element` (or `softwareSystem`) with the `External` tag is the
22:   correct representation of a third party — do not flag such an element for
23:   not being a `softwareSystem`.
24: - [ ] Each external system has a description explaining what it provides.
25: - [ ] No system is modeled that should actually be a container (e.g. a
26:   database you own).
27: - [ ] System names are unique and unambiguous.
28: 
29: ## Containers
30: 
31: - [ ] Every container represents a **runtime boundary** (a separately
32:   running process or a data store).
33: - [ ] No libraries, modules, or packages modeled as containers. A shared
34:   rules library, a JAR, a module, or a package is code-level: it runs inside
35:   another element's process and is not an element of its own. Finding one
36:   modeled as a container is an **Error** — name the container and say what
37:   level it actually belongs at.
38: - [ ] Every container has a technology specified.
39: - [ ] Every container has a meaningful description (not just restating the
40:   name, and not a bare list of technology names — "Technology Soup" is a
41:   description that is just technology names, where the description should
42:   state the responsibility).
43: - [ ] Database containers use the "Database" tag for the cylinder shape.
44: - [ ] No containers that should be external systems (services you don't own
45:   or deploy).
46: 
47: ## Components (if present)
48: 
49: - [ ] Components represent architecturally significant groupings, not just
50:   folder structure (the "Code Structure Mirror" — components that exactly
51:   match package or module structure model code organization, not
52:   architecture).
53: - [ ] Every component has a technology specified.
54: - [ ] Components are within a single container (not spanning containers).
55: - [ ] The component view adds genuine value (if not, recommend removing it —
56:   a stale component diagram that no longer matches the code is worse than
57:   none).
58: 
59: ## Completeness
60: 
61: - [ ] A missing relationship is a finding only when the model's own
62:   descriptions claim it (a description that names a counterpart the model has
63:   no edge to). Do not invent communication paths the model does not claim.
64: - [ ] No orphaned elements — elements with no relationships. The MCP
65:   `inspect` tool reports these as disconnected elements and as elements not
66:   included on any views; an orphan is a **Warning** (it is either dead weight
67:   or a relationship the model forgot) — name the element and say what is
68:   missing.
69: - [ ] A system context view and a container view exist at minimum (the
70:   "Missing Middle" — a system context view with no container view jumps
71:   straight to components).
72: 
73: ## Anti-patterns worth flagging
74: 
75: - **The "Docker Confusion"** — Docker containers modeled as C4 containers,
76:   or C4 containers modeled as Docker containers. C4 containers are runtime
77:   boundaries; Docker is a deployment mechanism (it belongs in the deployment
78:   view).
79: - **The "Technology Soup"** — element descriptions that are just technology
80:   names, where the description should state the responsibility.
